claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys is governed by a balance between configurational entropy and kinetically activated surface diffusion.
Configurational entropy favors a homogeneous mixed solid solution in high-entropy alloys, particularly as temperature increases.
Kinetically activated surface diffusion causes elemental segregation and phase decomposition in high-entropy nanoparticles.
Smaller nanoparticles have a higher surface-to-volume ratio than larger nanoparticles.
Smaller high-entropy nanoparticles will undergo elemental segregation and phase transitions earlier than larger particles under identical high-temperature conditions.
The proposed starting material is a well-mixed, metastable solid-solution nanoalloy with a uniform equiatomic or near-equiatomic composition.
High-temperature thermal activation enhances surface-diffusion kinetics.
The larger relative surface area of smaller nanoparticles accelerates elemental migration and segregation.
Surface segregation undermines the configurational-entropy stabilization of the mixed solid solution.
Larger nanoparticles retain the entropically stabilized mixed state longer and consequently show delayed or reduced segregation.
Relative to larger particles, smaller nanoalloys will exhibit earlier and more pronounced secondary-phase formation, diffraction changes, or EDS-detectable chemical segregation.
Larger high-entropy nanoparticles can retain a primarily homogeneous solid-solution state with minimal segregation during high-temperature exposure.
The predicted size dependence applies from approximately 600°C to 900°C under inert atmosphere at fixed composition.
Oxidizing environments or substantially different temperatures may alter the predicted size dependence.
Local defect density and interparticle interactions may influence high-temperature stability.
